World.title: Fizz takes three in Mumbai rout
World.content:
Pace sensation Mustafizur Rahman recorded his best bowling figures of the Indian Premier League today when he finished with 3 for 16 in Sunrisers Hyderabad’s 85-run victory over Mumbai Indians at Vishakhapatnam.

The three-wicket haul took the left-armer to joint-second in the wicket-takers’ list with a total tally of 13 scalps from nine matches. He is one short of Mitchell McClenaghan, who has taken 14 wickets in 10 matches.

The 20-year-old currently has the best bowling average, 15.61, and best economy rate, 6.15, amongs bowlers who have played at least eight matches in the tournament.

The Sunrisers Hyderabad might have depended on Mustafizur a number of times in the ongoing Indian Premier League, but today was a collective effort. Ashish Nehra, Bhuvaneshwar Kumar and Barinder Sran had reduced the Mumbai Indians to 49 for 6 in nine overs before Mustafizur was given the ball.

The wily left-armer sent back Hardik Pandya with his first ball with a cutter which Pandya failed to adjust himself against. Pandya attempted a slice through point, but the ball curled away to the hands of the keeper, with the umpire judging that out even though the television replays were inconclusive.

Then in the very first ball of his second over again, Fizz bowled yet another slower delivery which moved away from the batsman, getting the edge of Tim Southee on the way to the keeper.

The man from Satkhira returned got the scalp of McClenaghan in the final delivery of his third over, getting the batsman to offer a loopy catch to midwicket.

Mustafizur did not get to bowl a fourth over as David Warner gave the other bowlers their chance to mop up the tail. And they did efficiently, bundling out the hosts for just 92 runs in 16.3 overs.

Earlier, brilliant performances from Hyderabad openers, Warner and Shikhar Dhawan helped the team post 177. Dhawan scored 82 off 57 while Warner smacked 48 off 33. Yuvraj Singh also had a good time with the bat, scoring 39 off 23.

World.title: Fossickers accuse government of breaking promise to 'restore NT lifestyle'
World.content:
Fossickers have accused the Northern Territory government of breaking a key election promise to "restore the Territory lifestyle" with a plan to introduce fees and permits for the popular hobby.

The Country Liberal Party (CLP) won the 2024 NT election on the back of commitments to "reduce crime, rebuild the economy and restore the Territory lifestyle".

The government's Lifestyle Strategy 2025-2028 encourages Territorians to "fully enjoy our renowned outdoor activities, climate and natural environment" through "fishing, camping, bushwalking and a range of other outdoor and in-nature activities".

Matt Grambeau says there are as many as 1,000 fossickers in the Northern Territory. (ABC News: Pete Garnish )

But less than two years into its first term, the CLP has introduced legislation fossickers say contradicts the party's election platform.

The Mineral Titles Legislation Amendment Bill mainly aims to reduce red tape for mining and exploration companies, but it also explicitly proposes to increase red tape for recreational fossickers by introducing permits and yearly fees.

Most NT fossickers prospect for gold, with about 120 "passionate" treasure hunters out in the field every weekend. (ABC News: Pete Garnish )

NT Prospectors and Detectorists Association president Matt Grambeau said there were up to 1,000 recreational fossickers in the NT, most of whom prospect for gold, with around 120 "passionate fossickers … out there chasing minerals every weekend".

"You get to get out in the great outdoors, out into the territory, explore the bush and you never know what you're going to find," he said.

"It's a way of exercising, it's a form of mental health rehabilitation."

Matt Grambeau says fossicking is good exercise and benficial for prospectors' mental health. (ABC News: Pete Garnish )

Mr Grambeau said the fossicking community felt like they were being unfairly targeted by the legislation.

"The territory government has made a public commitment to restore and protect the Territory lifestyle," he said.

" We're struggling to understand how this bill aligns with that commitment. "

Fossickers use detectors to find gold and other minerals in the ground. (ABC News: Pete Garnish )

'There'd be an uproar'

Mr Grambeau said fossickers would be content with paying fees if the revenue raised was used to improve fossicking access or infrastructure.

But the bill does not specify how the extra revenue would be spent.

Mr Grambeau said fossickers already faced challenges accessing land in the NT, most of which is either Aboriginal-owned or covered by pastoral leases.

"We don't support the idea of paying a fee for something that we already do for free if we're not going to get any benefits derived from that fee," he said.

Nathan Wheeler is among roughly 1,000 fossickers that enjoy the NT's great outdoors through the hobby. (ABC News: Pete Garnish )

Mr Grambeau said there was a clear inconsistency with how the government treated fossickers, compared with fishers.

"Imagine if the government went to the fishing community of the Northern Territory and said: 'Hey, we are committed to restoring the Territory lifestyle and protecting the Territory lifestyle, but now you have to pay a fee to go fishing'," he said.

"'And we want to know where you're going and we want to increase offence provisions so if you do the wrong thing, there's going to be stricter compliance, and you're not going to get anything in return'.

"If the government said that to the fishing community, there'd be an uproar — it wouldn't be acceptable.

"There's definitely inconsistencies between one hobby and another hobby."

Matt Grambeau says the NT government is applying different standards for fossickers compared with other hobbyists. (ABC News: Pete Garnish )

Bill before scrutiny committee

The bill was introduced to NT parliament in March and was referred to the five-member Legislative Scrutiny Committee, which the government controls through a majority.

The committee has the power to recommend changes to the legislation, and will prepare a report before the bill returns to parliament in May.

Gerard Maley says fees for fossickers will be minimal. (ABC News: Dane Hirst )

In a statement, Mining Minister Gerard Maley said the bill would "create clearer, fairer rules for fossicking and other activities on private and public land".

"We understand recreational fossicking is part of the Territory lifestyle," he said.

"That is why any proposed fee would be minimal and focused on supporting better regulation, access and management of fossicking areas."

World.title: Live: PM to announce $45 million to fast-track housing, energy projects
World.content:
The global oil crisis sparked by war in the Middle East has dramatically exposed Australia's fuel vulnerabilities, sharpening calls from industry analysts for the federal government to secure future energy supplies.

Having secured shipments through to mid-May, attention is turning to how Labor will use next month's federal budget to shore up Australia's liquid fuel supply long term and reduce its dependence on volatile international markets.

The government has signalled energy security will be a key pillar of the budget, with members of the energy sector expecting fuel storage and refining capacity to be a focus for funding.

Read the full story from political reporter Nicole Asher in the link below.

World.title: Social media ad led dad to invest and watch savings 'crash and burn'
World.content:
Sydney father Leo thought he was pouring his money into investments that would one day help him buy a house.

While scrolling on Instagram in September, Leo, whose name has been changed for privacy reasons, came across a paid  for PrimeUPartner spruiking what he believed to be a legitimate high-yield investment platform.

After reading a few reviews online, which he now suspects were fraudulent, the 35-year-old invested $77,521 and was made to believe his investment had grown to $200,000 on the platform by December that year.

At the time, he was feeling optimistic and believed he was investing in cryptocurrency, stocks and even gold.

Wanting to cash in on his supposed winnings, Leo went to withdraw but when he tried to do so, he was told he had to make additional payments.

Leo says the fraudulent high yield investment platform has cost him years of savings. (ABC News: Abubakr Sajid)

Raising his suspicions and digging deeper, Leo discovered the entire platform, down to its graphs and numbers, was fake.

He had not made a single real investment.

"For it to completely crash and burn on me like that was just like horrific," he said.

Calls left unanswered

Leo's personal 'investment broker', who he had spent months talking to remotely and who had guided him through making 18 small instalments of cash into the website, would not call him back.

He said the scam had cost him years of savings.

Leo went to NSW Police in January this year, with officers confirming to the ABC the case was investigated and referred to Interpol's cyber fraud division.

He said he was not hopeful of getting back any of his lost funds.

Leo's case has been referred to Interpol's cyber-fraud division. (ABC News: Abubakr Sajid)

Former detective Blair Joynson has spent more than four years reviewing and investigating fraud and cyber crimes, with his business providing advisory on investigations for court matters, such as helping with cryptocurrency tracing.

Mr Joynson assisted Leo with contacting NSW Police.

Setting up a fraudulent high-yield investment platform had never been easier, Mr Joynson said, with cheap website templates available for purchase online.

"Then it becomes your ability to socially engineer people and to trick people really," he said.

Mr Joynson said investment scams like the one Leo experienced typically encouraged a victim to invest and then withdraw a small test amount, making them feel comfortable to then invest larger amounts.

The investments, which the victim may think are in cryptocurrency or other commodities, will then appear to be rising on the platform's website.

However, when they try to withdraw these seemingly successful investments, they are told they will need to pay extra transactions or processing fees and contact with the platform will go dark.

Blair Joyston says setting up a fraudulent high-yield investment platform has never been easier for scammers. (Supplied: Conseek)

Mr Joynson said he had seen hundreds of cases like Leo's play out and said almost all of them had originated from social media.

A report by the National Anti-Scam Centre found investment scams continued to result in the most significant financial harm to Australians, with combined losses of $837.7 million in 2025.

In 2025, the National Anti-Scam Centre collaborated with the Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC) to disrupt investment scams, which included the removal of fake investment platforms, phishing scams, cryptocurrency investment scams and investment scam s on social media.

Mr Joynson said scammers often paid for Meta s — the parent company of Facebook and Instagram — to lure people to their fraudulent platform.

The ABC contacted Meta for comment.

Many Australians use social media as a source of financial information. (ABC News: Abbey Haberecht)

Efforts were made to contact PrimeUPartner, though its website is now defunct, coming up as a "certificate error", indicating that a browser cannot verify the website's SSL certificate was issued by a trusted certificated authority.

An SSL certificate is a digital certificate that authenticates a website's identity and enables a safe, encrypted connection.

Social media a source of financial information for many

According to a survey by ASIC released last month, 63 per cent of 18-to 28-year-olds said they used social media as a source of financial information.

That figure was higher than those who used professional financial services or sought advice from family and friends, the results found.

Another 40 per cent reported they had been messaged directly by someone encouraging them to invest.

ASIC also took down more than 1,100 online investment scam s on social media in 2025.

ASIC's Alan Kirkland warned of fradulent activity on social media platforms. (ABC News: Michael Nudl)

"I think it shows that there's a lot of activity that's happening, often under the radar, encouraging people to make crypto investments," Commissioner Alan Kirkland said.

"One of the risks as a consumer is sometimes it's hard to know which of those are actual crypto assets and which might be a scam because we've seen a number of scams that have seen people lose their money."

For Leo, the experience of losing almost $78,000 had been deeply distressing.

"I wanted to buy a home and set my family up. That was the goal this year," he said.

"All my savings are completely gone, I've got no money, so I'm just starting back from scratch."

World.title: How self-employment can help autistic people avoid workplace challenges
World.content:
For Warragul woman Carmel Riley, self-employment provided an opportunity to grow.

Ms Riley had never considered entrepreneurship, but after undertaking a Master of Business Administration (MBA) and working across different industries, she realised she had never fitted in at other workplaces.

"My personality, my character, the way I viewed the world, the fact that I was a mother — there was no end to the reasons that I never quite fit necessarily in the different organisations that I worked with," Ms Riley said.

In 2019, she founded a consultancy, which grew to become Consulting Reimagined Social Enterprise (CRSE) Group, providing advisory services to other social enterprises and not-for-profit organisations, as well as governments and larger companies.

Though her autism was undiagnosed at the time, Ms Riley realised after founding CRSE Group that being self-employed was working well for her and her needs.

Last year, the federal government released Australia's first National Autism Strategy, a document that sets out a path to improve the lives of Australians with autism.

Carmel Riley says she learnt how to create psychologically safe workplaces during her period of self-employment. (ABC News: Danielle Kutchel)

A Department of Health, Disability and Ageing spokesperson said the strategy’s focus on self-employment and entrepreneurship was driven by community consultation, acknowledging that many autistic people started their own businesses due to the barriers they faced in workplaces and an ability to find creative solutions to problems.

According to the Australian Bureau of Statistics, the unemployment rate for autistic people of working age was 18.2 per cent, more than double the rate for people with disability (7.5 per cent) and almost six times the rate of people without disability (3.1 per cent).

Why self-employment works

Victoria's peak body for people with autism, Amaze, said autistic people faced systemic barriers to employment and experienced higher levels of discrimination and bullying in the workplace.

The organisation said autistic people were less likely to be hired, while workplace norms, a lack of understanding around autism, and stigmas and stereotypes meant autistic people were more likely to lose a job once hired.

Inflexible work arrangements, high noise levels, crowded spaces, bright lights, and other issues in traditional workplaces can lead to overstimulation for people with autism, ending in autistic burnout and ongoing health problems.

Ms Riley said self-employment helped get around those barriers.

"That's the other beautiful thing around self-employment for neurodivergence. You can actually create the environments that you can thrive in and deliver really good quality products and services," she said.

It can also allow autistic people to work in their area of special interest, a term used to describe a subject that a neurodivergent person is intensely passionate and deeply knowledgeable about, and able to hyper-focus on for extended periods of time.

This is the case for Ms Riley's daughter, Matilda, who identifies as neurodivergent.

Two years ago, with the encouragement of her mother, she created a small arts and crafts business, Made by Matilda: No One Owns Colours.

Matilda Riley has started a small business selling her artwork. (ABC News: Danielle Kutchel)

She sells colourful paintings and postcards and has tried her hand at sewing scrunchies, and hopes she can one day begin selling at local craft markets.

To do her best work, she makes sure she has a clear, quiet space and her tools organised and ready to go, so she can work without interruption.

Uncontrolled noise causes her to lose focus and become overwhelmed, so being able to control that in her own environment helps.

"It just kind of gives me a chance to relax and not think about everything," she said.

"It's really fun."

Supporting autistic entrepreneurs

Sharon Zivkovic, an autistic researcher and founder of Community Capacity Builders and the Centre for Autistic Social Entrepreneurship, said autistic ways of thinking lent themselves to innovation and entrepreneurship.

She creates neurodiversity-affirming advisory programs to support other autistic entrepreneurs.

Her programs are also designed for mainstream business advisers and other services that work with innovators, and Dr Zivkovic said it was important that these services recognised what she called "autistic cognition".

Sharon Zivkovic says autistic ways of thinking lend themselves to innovation and entrepreneurship. (Supplied: Sharon Zivkovic)

"In the programs that I've developed, I highlight the fact that we've got these databases in our heads for our interest areas — the research shows we're bottom-up thinkers, not top down," she said.

"We're associative thinkers [and] we're recognised as systemisers. We can see all of the bits that can come together to make something work, because that's just our natural cognition."

Autism diagnosis sparks career change After Tom Sheppard was diagnosed with autism, a program designed for Australians on the spectrum helped him land a job that plays to his strengths.

She said if the government was serious about delivering on its commitment through the National Autism Strategy, it needed to make sure business advisers and disability services understood the way autistic people thought about business.

Last year, the federal government commissioned a review into the effectiveness of existing autism-specific employment programs, which led to a grant opportunity opened earlier this year to develop and promote autism-specific employment training.

The successful applicant is expected to be announced soon.

Ms Zivkovic said these services needed to recognise that self-employment could offer big benefits to autistic people.

"The only way we're going to be able to overcome burnout and other kinds of issues is by controlling our work environment, and you can't control your work environment if you're working for someone else," she said.

A learning experience

Ms Riley said she had learnt a lot about leadership during her time running CRSE Group.

Several CRSE staff members disclosed their own neurodivergence to Ms Riley and thanked her for creating a safe space where they could thrive in their employment.

"If you can create that environment of psychological safety, it's amazing what you can unlock in your people," she said.

Ms Riley said the government could encourage autistic entrepreneurs by supporting autistic-led businesses through social procurement strategies.

"Give us a chance to deliver you business. That's all we need," she said.

World.title: Questions loom over LIV Golf's future, but a multi-million dollar course upgrade is playing through
World.content:
International media reports of LIV Golf's impending doom have left the Malinauskas government staring down a Hamlet without the Prince moment — a performance without its star.

The government officially took control of the North Adelaide public golf course on Monday to start work on a $45 million redevelopment, which will have the course ready to host the Saudi-backed LIV Golf tour in 2028.

That is if there is any LIV Golf to host.

The concept design for the golf course's redevelopment. (Supplied: SA government)

The Financial Times and Wall Street Journal reported earlier this month that Saudi Arabia's sovereign wealth fund was on the verge of cutting its support for LIV Golf after years of sustaining hundreds of millions in losses.

The state government said it had received "assurances" from LIV Golf, while the league's CEO said the tournament was "funded through the season" but work was required beyond that "to keep us going".

If the money from Saudi Arabia dries up, does the case for redeveloping North Adelaide too?

That is the line of questioning Premier Peter Malinauskas and his ministers have been fielding over the past two weeks.

The government has been consistent from day one that redeveloping North Adelaide was about much more than LIV Golf, highlighting that the "world class" course will be a tourist attraction open to the public for the rest of the year.

The North Adelaide golf course has views of the Adelaide CBD. (ABC News: Carl Saville)

But it is also worth considering these comments from the premier in February 2025, when he announced both the North Adelaide redevelopment and LIV Golf staying in SA until 2031.

"We think that timeline's the perfect one that sets us up for the future," Mr Malinauskas said at the time.

"That also justifies the investment — we didn't want to invest heavily in North Adelaide and face the prospect of it being lost from South Australia.

"This gives us the security that it requires to be able to justify that investment."

Without that security, is the investment justified?

The project's most outspoken critics, like Greens MLC Robert Simms, argue no.

"The government only ever committed to this project on the basis that it was going to be supposedly the jewel in the crown for LIV Golf," Mr Simms said, claiming the project's business case "evaporates" without LIV.

Greens MLC Robert Simms is concerned about the effect on the park lands and the association with the Saudi government. (ABC News: Tony Hill)

But the government is firmly standing by its course.

"Our investment in the public golf course is ultimately an investment in public community use infrastructure," Mr Malinauskas said on Monday.

"Although LIV Golf underpins one of the reasons why we're investing in the golf course, 51 weeks of the year it's there for the public of South Australia to use, and in growing numbers.

"That still stacks up regardless."

The premier also said the course would host other golf tournaments, like the already locked-in Women's Australian Open.

"There may yet be other opportunities in the event something does happen to LIV," he added.

No turning back now

LIV Golf has plenty of support in SA — one only has to look at its success in Adelaide to see that, with the event in Grange one of the tour's biggest money-spinners.

And even if the government wanted to change tack, it is hard to see how they would back out now given the amount of political capital they have already invested in it.

As North Adelaide Golf Club president Kevin Naughton observed, the plans to redevelop the course have been around "for almost 30 years".

"It's now started and once it's started it's unstoppable," he said.

The government getting to this point involved a nasty spat with Adelaide City Council — who were largely cut out of the project via special legislation — and a politically fraught Aboriginal heritage process.

Protesters accuse the premier of cutting down trees in North Adelaide without justification. (ABC News: Angelique Donnellan)

The concerns from park lands advocates about the impact on trees have never abated either.

After months of pre-election speculation about how many were facing the chop, the government revealed in December that it would fell 585 trees but plant 1,700 replacements.

The Adelaide Park Lands Association held a "vigil" for the soon-to-be felled trees — protest images which led the evening news coverage on Monday as the project kicked off.

Protesters against the redevelopment of the golf course on the day it was handed over to the state government. (ABC News: Angelique Donnellan)

When the premier announced the North Adelaide golf course project last year, he put it in the category of a calculated risk.

It might still pay off, but the uncertainty around LIV's future means the risk has arguably never been higher.

World.title: Don't assume El Niño warming will bring record heat
World.content:
The Pacific Ocean's continued rapid warming towards El Niño has firmed up the odds that Australia faces a warm and dry second half to 2026.

And forecasts continue to upgrade El Niño's potential strength, with the Bureau of Meteorology's (BOM) latest modelling tipping a record event.

But thankfully for Australia, a record El Niño does not suggest record drought or heat, with previous events showing only a weak relationship between strength and severity of impacts.

Pacific warming at a near record rate

Analysis from the central Pacific, El Niño's engine room, shows water temperatures have already climbed more than 1 degree Celsius since January, the greatest rate of warming this century and the most rapid transition from La Niña to El Niño since 1976.

But in 1976, warming eventually stalled, and it became only a weak or borderline event, which the BOM does not even classify as a fully-fledged El Niño.

This year, however, El Niño has the potential to break records.

The NIÑO3.4 index, the most commonly used yardstick for the state of the Pacific, is now +0.23C and could reach the BOM's El Niño threshold of +0.8C within weeks, although a declaration will not be made until there is clear evidence the atmosphere has responded.

This would represent a much earlier emergence of El Niño compared to normal. For example, during the 2023 El Niño, the 0.8C mark was not exceeded until September.

Because El Niños follow a standard seasonal cycle, an autumn or early winter onset allows more time for strengthening before a peak arrives in spring or summer.

"Climate models are now strongly aligned and there is high confidence in the onset of El Niño, followed by further intensification in the months that follow," chief of climate prediction at the World Meteorological Organization, Wilfran Moufouma-Okia said.

The BOM's model ACCESS-S is tipping the Niño3.4 index will soar to an unprecedented +2.9C in October, comfortably a new record for the oceanic strength of the El Niño signal.

And while the BOM's model is one of the more aggressive, a survey of leading global forecasts shows the general consensus also favours a significant event in 2026 with a NIÑO3.4 peak of around +1.5C to +2C, still considered a strong or very strong (super) El Niño.

But stronger events do not necessarily mean more severe impacts in Australia, according to University of New South Wales climate scientist Andrea Taschetto.

One of the strongest El Niño events in 1997/98 only had a modest impact on Australian rainfall, while the weak El Niño event of 2002/03 coincided with severe drought.

Why do we care about El Niño?

El Niño is one of the world's most influential climate drivers, helping to rearrange weather systems around the globe.

"Australia, it's very close to where El Niño happens, so the impacts for Australia are really significant," Dr Taschetto said.

Every event is different, with a number of factors working to pull the strings on the weather and climate.

But, in general, El Niño events see drier and warmer weather across northern and eastern Australia, particularly from June to November.

El Niño has been linked to some of the worst droughts in modern history, including the millennium drought between 1997 and 2010. This photo from the time is titled "Drought, Continuing Drought'. (Supplied: Julie Millowick)

Nine of the 10 driest winter–spring periods on record for eastern Australia occurred during El Niño years, according to the BOM.

This influence means it is often associated with drought, extreme heat and bushfires.

Driest April in decades drops soil moisture

This drying influence means good rains in autumn become more critical. However, a wet March is now a distant memory for much of Australia.

Much of Australia has failed to see significant rainfall in April, especially across the interior and eastern inland. (ABC News)

About a third of the country has failed to receive even a millimetre this month, and for several regions of eastern Australia April is on track to become the driest in decades.

In Gippsland, Bairnsdale has only picked up 5mm, the lowest April total since 1943.

Lithgow in central NSW has only received 2mm, the driest April since 1899, while Glen Innes in the state's north is stuck on 0mm for the first time since 1942.

The lack of rain in the New England region follows below average precipitation through summer, leading to record low soil moisture and the emergence of drought.

In southern Queensland, Texas and Toowoomba have both seen their driest April's since the 1990s.

Uncertainty of autumn as oceans undergo reset

But it is not all doom and gloom as forecasts early in the year can be inaccurate, and a dry April in isolation is not a reliable indication of a dry winter or spring.

Climate scientists and the BOM are notably cautious talking about El Niño's potential arrival or influence at this time of year.

This is because of something known as the "autumn predictability barrier", where just one unexpected weather event in the Pacific, such as a late-season cyclone or a strong burst of winds, can disrupt the development of a looming El Niño.

The ocean undergoes a 'reset' during autumn, which makes it susceptible to small fluctuations in the weather than during the other months (ABC: Chris Lewis)

"It's a really hard time of the year to be predicting those things just because it's a transition season," Dr Taschetto said.

In 2014, for example, early forecasts were projecting a strong El Niño event.

Then a persistent stream of easterly winds over the Pacific stopped it from happening.

"Then next year, 2015 and 16, was a massive El Niño event that came in the end," Dr Taschetto said.

No strong dry signal in winter outlook yet

While El Niño is a big player in the world of weather, current forecasts do not paint a dramatic picture of Australia's climate in the months to come.

The BOM's latest long range forecast for the winter months shows a slightly increased chance of "unusually dry" conditions for parts of south-eastern Australia and south-western Australia.

Despite early signs of an El Niño, the BOM's long-range outlook for winter rainfall does not look overly dry across Australia. (Supplied: BOM)

Elsewhere, there is no clear dry signal.

The strongest sign in the outlook is for winter daytime temperatures, which are very likely to be warmer than normal for most of the country outside the tropics.

Daytime temperatures in winter are highly likely to be warmer than normal, according to early long-range forecast from the BOM (Supplied: BOM)

El Niño gives hints beyond the outlook

There is no official long-range forecast beyond August, but typically El Niño favours lower spring rainfall for most of the country's east, and warmer than normal temperatures.

"[The El Niño Southern Oscillation] accounts for up to 40 per cent of the precipitation variability from September to November. So, it's a significant number," Dr Taschetto said.

Unlike its 'sister', La Niña, El Niño's influence on rainfall doesn't typically extend into our summer, but warmer conditions lag until at least January or February.

However, since every event is different, the BOM encourages people to watch the long-range forecast, which captures the specific nuances of all climate drivers, a far more accurate measure of potential weather than El Niño alone.

World.title: What we know about the hours before a 5yo girl went missing in Alice Springs
World.content:
Late on Saturday night, a five-year-old girl vanished from a home in an Alice Springs town camp, sparking a desperate search.

In the days since, as Sharon Granites's disappearance has made national headlines and the search for her has expanded, a clearer picture of what happened that night has emerged.

Here's what we know so far.

The house where Sharon Granites was last seen in Old Timers town camp, in Alice Springs. (ABC News: Will Green)

Saturday was a warm autumn day in Alice Springs, when Sharon and her mother visited a home at the Old Timers / Ilyperenye Aboriginal camp on the outskirts of the regional town.

The town camp is a small community, with only nine households and about 40 residents, which is maintained by the local Aboriginal corporation Tangentyere Council.

Old Timers town camp is a small community situated between the Alice Springs town centre and the suburb of Kilgariff. (ABC News Graphics: Jessica Henderson)

Police say Sharon and her mother were visiting the home of some people they knew well, to do some Saturday laundry.

As the evening went on, police say a party was held at the house for a "social occasion", with several people in attendance.

One of those people was Jefferson Lewis, a 47-year-old man who was staying at the home at Old Timers after having been released from prison six days prior.

Police are searching for Jefferson Lewis in relation to the alleged abduction. (Supplied: NT Police Force)

At some point that night, police say they visited the town camp for an unrelated incident and captured footage of Mr Lewis on officers' body-worn cameras.

The grainy photos from that night's footage show Mr Lewis wearing a bright yellow shirt and a grey and yellow cap.

Police say their interaction with Mr Lewis that night was "fortuitous" and that "no offence" had occurred at that time, with police leaving the location shortly after.

Jefferson Lewis was at Old Timers town camp the night Sharon went missing. (Supplied: NT Police Force)

But at 11pm that night, police say Mr Lewis was seen by those in the area for the last time, and he was with a little girl believed to be Sharon.

"He was last seen with the little girl holding hands," police said on Tuesday.

Just before 11:30pm, Sharon was put into bed by family at the house that she and her mother were visiting. She was wearing a dark blue short-sleeved T-shirt with a white ring stripe around the neck and cuffs and a pair of black boxer-style underwear.

That was the last time anyone saw her.

Sharon Granites was last seen on Saturday night, by family members. (Supplied: NT Police Force )

A little later, Sharon's mother went to check on her little girl in the bedroom she was sleeping in and found that she had vanished.

At 1:30am, the distraught mother called NT Police and reported Sharon missing.

Police now believe that Mr Lewis "led that little girl away" from the home.

From a young girl who 'wandered off' to a suspected abduction

After arriving at Old Timers town camp in the early hours of Sunday morning, police spent hours conducting a search of the area.

Police initially told the media they believed Sharon might have "wandered off" through an unlocked door.

Throughout the rest of the day, a search party of more than 50 police officers, as well as members of the NT Emergency Service, looked for the five-year-old in the surrounding area, including along the dry Todd River, which is adjacent to the town camp.

NT Emergency Service members searching the dry riverbed of the Todd for any sign of Sharon Granites. (ABC News: Will Green )

With no luck overnight, on Monday morning, police recommenced a foot and air search of the area, with the help of the force's elite Territory Response Group (TRG).

History of man police are searching for over 5yo missing girl A man being sought in connection with the alleged abduction of five-year-old Sharon Granites near Alice Springs has a long history of violence and prison time in the Northern Territory.

By 9:30am on Monday, police announced to the media they believed Sharon had been abducted and were searching for Mr Lewis in relation to her disappearance.

Later that day, Mr Lewis's long history of violence and repeated stints in NT prisons over the last decade was reported in the media.

Among his past offences were serious assaults, contraventions of domestic violence orders, breaches of bail and acts of resisting police.

The search continued on Tuesday, including through dense scrubland. Speaking at a press conference that morning, police said despite two days of search efforts yielding no results, they believed the five-year-old girl was still alive.

Peter Malley says police believe Sharon Granites is still alive. (ABC News: Will Green)

NT Police Assistant Commissioner for Crime and Intelligence Peter Malley said the girl's suspected abduction had been declared a major crime and finding her was the force's "number one priority".

Assistant Commissioner Malley added that the case was "one of the biggest investigations [the NT's] had going for a while", with the "TRG, motorbikes, horses, helicopters, drones" all having been deployed for the search effort, as well as Aboriginal trackers.

Horses, dogs and helicopters have all been used in the search for the missing girl. (ABC News: Will Green)

The assistant commissioner said a fugitive task force had also been called to Alice Springs to assist on Tuesday.

The NT Police Force's executive director of cultural reform, Leanne Liddle, said the mother of the five-year-old girl was "distraught" and was going through "every parent's worst nightmare".

Police are continuing to call on anyone with information about Sharon or Mr Lewis to contact them, no matter "how small in detail you think it may be".

World.title: Cotton growers furious as dam expansion dumped over wetland fears
World.content:
As drought conditions challenge western NSW, the state government's plan to balance water security while protecting an endangered marshland has drawn criticism from farmers.

The Macquarie River is the main source of irrigation water for farmers throughout the Macquarie Valley, a major producer of cotton and cereals.

The river also supplies the internationally protected Macquarie Marshes, one of Australia's largest waterbird breeding sites.

Burrendong Dam regulates water flows for farms as well as supplying nearby towns.

The dam sat almost empty when the drought broke in January 2020, before filling above capacity within 18 months.

Burrendong Dam was below 2 per cent capacity in 2020. (Supplied: Mick Williams/Inland Waterways OzFish)

As the dam level drops again amid the latest dry spell, increasing the dam's capacity has emerged as a popular option to improve water security.

However, the NSW government has recently confirmed it will not be proceeding with the option due to concerns over environmental impact.

"There was a number of recommendations that came through from the last drought to improve water security in the Macquarie Valley, and all of these have been knocked on the head besides bores for Dubbo," Macquarie Cotton Growers' Association president Richie Quigley said.

Richie Quigley (left) and politician Scott Barrett are questioning the decision to reject the Burrendong proposal (Supplied)

" Bores provide greater water security for Dubbo, which is a good thing, but it doesn't help any of the downstream towns that were really on the brink and suffered severely during the last drought. "

Multi-million-dollar water investigation

Since 2024, multiple options to improve water reliability for communities such as Dubbo, Warren, Nyngan and Cobar, while maintaining the river environment, have been investigated as part of the $9.35 million Macquarie Wambuul Water Security Project.

The NSW Department of Climate Change, Energy, Environment and Water (DCCEEW) led the project, consulting the community on four options: a pipeline between Dubbo and Nyngan, replacing the Gin Gin weir, improving groundwater access for Dubbo, and using part of Burrendong Dam's flood mitigation storage to increase supply.

Burrendong Dam spilled over in 2022, with 8,000 gigalitres being released a day. (Supplied: Water NSW)

The Burrendong proposal was the most popular during public consultation, with supporters arguing it would capture only a small portion of excess floodwater to deliver significant benefits during drought.

The flood mitigation zone is the extra empty space above the dam's normal full level available to temporarily capture incoming floodwater that can be controlled to reduce flooding downstream.

Supporters argue that capturing more water during floods, like in 2022 (pictured), will improve water security. (Supplied: Beryl Carberry)

"It will store more water during wet times to use during the dry using the infrastructure we already have," Mr Quigley said.

"Particularly during periods when there's so much water and it's doing damage to communities, properties, riparian zones."

Warren mayor Greg Whiteley also supported the Burrendong option, saying an extra 200 gigalitres of water would provide a year's water supply for critical human needs for these towns during a drought crisis.

A DCCEEW spokesperson said raising dam limit was "thoroughly assessed".

"While this option would improve town water security, it was not shortlisted to move to the next phase as it would deliver limited, uncertain benefits at a high and irreversible environmental cost," they said.

'Blatant water grab'

Mel Gray from the grassroots water advocacy group Healthy Rivers Dubbo said raising the dam level would deprive water from the Marshes, which is an endangered ecological community.

"This scientifically-achieved classification means that community has a very high risk of extinction within 20 years," she said.

" Floods aren't a big damaging thing to fear, if you cut them short, a sudden drop in water is a way to guarantee the rapid extinction to the bird population. "

The Macquarie Marshes are a stark reality of the water crisis in NSW. (Supplied: Ryan Shields)

The Burrendong proposal was also opposed for undermining the ability to protect towns during a major flood.

"On Friday, November 26, 2022, a record 220 thousand megalitres flowed into Burrendong dam; that's almost half of the flood mitigation zone size," Ms Gray said.

"If the flood mitigation zone had not been available, significant flooding would have been experienced in Wellington, Dubbo, Narromine and other communities downstream of the dam."

Mel Gray says the dam proposal is reckless in withholding water from the environment. (Supplied)

" The proposal to reduce the flood mitigation zone in Burrendong dam, exposing all residents along the flood plain downstream of Burrendong dam to increased risk of flooding, is reckless. "

Rose Jackson is being asked to publicly share the modelling. (ABC Western Plains: Kenji Sato)

In response to requests from the public for greater transparency about the decision-making process, a spokesperson for Water Minister Rose Jackson said some of the data used to make the decision would soon be shared.

"Minister Jackson's office and the DCCEEW are working to produce a summary of the full business case that we can share with the public," a statement read.

"That will help explain the process and how government came to shortlist the preferred option of securing groundwater for Dubbo."

World.title: King Charles just told Trump exactly what he needed to hear – but it may not be enough
World.content:
Analysis WorldEuropeKing Charles III King Charles just told Trump exactly what he needed to hear – but it may not be enough David Crowe April 29, 2026 — 7:05am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

London: King Charles used the power of the podium at the US Congress to deliver a gentle but compelling message to Donald Trump and the American people about the value of remembering their friends. The King’s address was serious, persuasive and incredibly sly in the way it told the US President what his many critics think he needs to hear. King Charles addressing the US Congress on Tuesday. Getty Images But even a superb speech, surrounded by the high ceremony of a state visit, will not be enough to restore the “special relationship” between Britain and America when Trump is not likely to listen. This was a very clever speech. At a time of war with Iran, the King spoke of fostering compassion and promoting peace. At a time of concern about presidential power, he spoke of the Magna Carta and its core principle that executive power is subject to checks and balances. He emphasised respect for people of different faiths.



At a time when Trump dismisses climate change, the King spoke of the “disastrously melting ice-caps of the Arctic” and the need to safeguard nature. With a nod to Australia, he urged support for the AUKUS pact. He also addressed the doubts about Trump’s allegiances in Europe by calling for more support for Ukraine – and getting sustained applause from Congress. The King with US President Donald Trump on Tuesday. AP Every message was crafted so carefully, and spoken so mildly, that it would have been churlish for anyone to point out that the King was being political. His most important task, however, was to bond the American and British people together in a way that might survive Trump’s complaints about the alliance. He probably achieved this to some extent, given the audience inside and outside the Congress, and this alone gives his address a significant value.



“The challenges we face are too great for any one nation to bear alone,” he said. Throughout the speech, the King argued against the isolationist streak in American politics and against the “might is right” approach that defines the Trump administration. Will this save the special relationship? No. It does not hurt for the King and the president to project friendship and common purpose with all the glamour of the ceremonial visit. Loading It is wise, however, not to put too much weight on what we see. The US visit simply repeats the cycle we saw last year when Trump enjoyed a very successful state visit to the UK. Back then, the magic of the monarchy certainly had its effect on the president when he and his wife, Melania, arrived at Windsor Castle. He appeared to soften in the presence of the unfailingly polite royal family, as he enjoyed a banquet in St George’s Hall with the Princess of Wales on his right and the King on his left.





The remarks about allied forces were deeply offensive in Britain, as they were in Australia. The King, as ceremonial head of the armed forces, would be justified in rebuking Trump and reminding him of the soldiers of the Commonwealth who died in those conflicts. But the biggest argument is the most recent one: Trump’s expectation that the UK, and other NATO allies, should have joined him in his decision to launch airstrikes on Iran in tandem with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Starmer dithered over his response: he refused US access to British bases, then allowed it for defensive operations. His most important decision, however, was in line with every other European leader: none of them joined the war. NATO, the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation, was not going to be turned into an offensive pact to start fights in the Middle East. While almost every NATO leader learned from the mistakes in Afghanistan and Iraq over the past two decades, one of them did not. Trump is now caught in an Iranian quagmire – and his only committed ally is Netanyahu.



Related Article Royal family US has ‘no closer friend’ than Britain, Trump says as he welcomes Charles In an unguarded moment, a British diplomat confirmed this reality to a private group of students in February. “I think there is probably one country that has a special relationship with the United States, and that is probably Israel,” said Christian Turner, who is now the UK ambassador to the US. This was reported by The Financial Times on Tuesday. The remark made news because it captures the overwhelming sense of a lasting divide between Trump’s America and the old allies, especially Britain. Smiles and ceremonies can hide some of the divisions for a few days, but they cannot make the underlying problem go away. Nor can a king’s speech, not matter how cleverly it is crafted. On the surface, the British relationship with America looked solid and, frankly, a little glamorous with the arrival of royalty in the US capital. Below the surface, there is a structural gulf in the way the two countries see the world.

World.title: ‘It’s not OK to steal a charity’: Elon Musk takes stand in blockbuster trial
World.content:
Breaking TechnologyCourts ‘It’s not OK to steal a charity’: Elon Musk takes stand in blockbuster trial Barbara Ortutay Updated April 29, 2026 — 6:42am ,first published 5:40am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

California: Elon Musk, the Tesla CEO, world’s richest man and OpenAI cofounder, took the stand on Tuesday (US time) in a high-stakes trial revolving around a bitter feud between himself and former friends Sam Altman and Greg Brockman that could reshape the future development of artificial intelligence. The bickering billionaires’ are at the Oakland federal courthouse for the start of a legal drama that is expected to brim with intrigue and potentially embarrassing details about the two tech moguls. Musk filed the lawsuit against Altman and Brockman along with Microsoft over its investments in OpenAI, in 2024. Elon Musk arrives at the federal courthouse in Oakland, California. AP “Fundamentally, I think they’re going to try to make this lawsuit...very complicated, but it’s actually very simple,” Musk said. “Which is that it’s not OK to steal a charity.” Musk, who founded automaker Tesla and rocket company SpaceX, also said he is committed to serving the public, by working 80- to 100-hour weeks and generally not taking vacations. “I like working and solving problems that make people’s lives better,” he said.



The jury was elected Monday and the trial is scheduled to take three weeks. Opening arguments began with Musk’s attorney, Steven Molo, who quoted OpenAI’s mission statement when it was created as a nonprofit for the benefit of humanity as a whole and not constrained by the need to generate financial enrichment for anyone. Altman and his top lieutenant Brockman, aided by Microsoft, “stole a charity,” Molo said, “a charity whose mission was the safe, open development of artificial intelligence.” Related Article Opinion

AI AI heavyweights’ court battle could unravel the entire sector Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist In the civil lawsuit, Musk, the world’s richest person with an estimated fortune of $US778 billion ($1.08 trillion), accuses Altman and Brockman of double-crossing him by straying from the San Francisco company’s founding mission to be a steward of a revolutionary technology. He is seeking damages and to fund the altruistic efforts of OpenAI’s charitable arm and Altman’s ouster from OpenAI’s board.



OpenAI has brushed off Musk’s allegations as an unfounded case of sour grapes that’s aimed at undercutting its rapid growth and bolstering Musk’s own xAI, which he launched in 2023 as a competitor. In his opening statement, OpenAI lawyer William Savitt told jurors “we are here because Mr. Musk didn’t get his way with OpenAI.” Sam Altman inside the courthouse on Tuesday. Bloomberg Savitt said Musk wanted “the keys to the kingdom,” and sued only after he failed and then in 2023 started his own AI business, xAI, now part of SpaceX. “ Savitt said Musk used his promises to provide funding to bully OpenAI founding members and tried to take control of OpenAI and merge it with Tesla. In fact, he said Musk wanted to form a for-profit company and own more than 50 per cent of it. In the middle of discussions about OpenAI’s future, he added, Musk pulled the plug on $US5 million quarterly donations he was making.



There is no record, Savitt said, of promises made to Musk that OpenAI was going to remain a nonprofit forever, or open-source everything. What Musk ultimately cared about, he said, was not OpenAI’s nonprofit status but winning the AI race with Google. Molo said the case is not about Musk, but rather Altman, Brockman and Microsoft. ‘Fundamentally, I think they’re going to try to make this lawsuit...very complicated, but it’s actually very simple. Which is that it’s not OK to steal a charity.’ Elon Musk By 2017, about two years after OpenAI’s founding, it became clear that OpenAI would need more money, and Molo said the founders eventually settled on the idea of creating a for-profit arm of OpenAI that would support the nonprofit. Terms were capped for investors so they “couldn’t make infinite profit.” “There is nothing wrong with a nonprofit having a for-profit subsidiary, but (it) has to advance the mission,” Molo said.



Microsoft initially invested $US2 billion in OpenAI. Then, in 2022, news spread that OpenAI had done a deal with Microsoft and “this was a horse of a completely different colour,” he said. It was a “gamechanger,” Molo said, that violated “every commitment” OpenAI made not just to Musk but to the world. It was no longer open source, it became a for-profit company for the benefit of the defendants and Microsoft was going to have control, through licensing, of much of its intellectual property, Molo said. Related Article Billionaires ‘Crazy and nasty’: Secrets revealed as the world’s richest man and his rival go to war Musk’s side is expected to present a tale chock-full of alleged betrayal, deceit and ambition that caused OpenAI to pivot from its founding mission as an altruistic startup to a capitalistic venture now valued at $US852 billion. Altman, OpenAI’s CEO, is also expected to testify, along with Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, one of the technology leaders who helped fund the late 2022 release of ChatGPT, the chatbot that unleashed the current AI boom that has propelled the stock market to record heights. Altman’s court appearance likely made him unavailable to attend an Amazon event across San Francisco Bay on Tuesday at which both companies announced an expanded partnership.



“I wish I could be there with you in person today,” Altman told attendees of Amazon’s event in San Francisco via a prerecorded video message. “My schedule got taken away from me today.” More to come AP, wires The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. Sign up to get it every weekday morning.

World.title: ASX set to fall as sinking AI stocks weigh down Wall Street; UAE to leave OPEC oil cartel
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to fall as sinking AI stocks weigh down Wall Street; UAE to leave OPEC oil cartel Stan Choe Updated April 29, 2026 — 6:40am ,first published 5:15am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Sinking AI stocks and another climb in oil prices because of the Iran war helped pull Wall Street off its record heights on Tuesday. The S&P 500 fell 0.5 per cent from its latest all-time high. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 25 points, or 0.1 per cent, while the Nasdaq composite fell 0.9 per cent from its own record. The drops for artificial intelligence stocks came after a report in The Wall Street Journal said some leaders at OpenAI are concerned about whether it can support its massive spending on data centres after missing targets for new users and revenue. Bloomberg The Australian sharemarket is set to decline, with futures at 4.56am AEST pointing to a loss of 33 points, or 0.4 per cent, at the open. The ASX lost 0.6 per cent on Tuesday. The Australian dollar was trading at US71.85¢. The Australian Bureau of Statistics on Wednesday will release the March consumer price index with analysts united in expecting a petrol-induced surge in prices that will take the overall inflation rate towards 5 per cent. Stocks in the artificial-intelligence industry led the way lower on Wall Street. Chip company Broadcom was the heaviest weight on the S&P 500 after sinking 4.4 per cent. Drops of 1.6 per cent for Nvidia and 3.9 per cent for Micron Technology also undercut the market.



Related Article Opinion

AI AI heavyweights’ court battle could unravel the entire sector Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist The weakness came after a report in The Wall Street Journal said some leaders at OpenAI are concerned about whether it can support its massive spending on data centres after missing targets for new users and revenue. If the maker of ChatGPT pulls back on its investments, it could bolster criticism that the entire AI industry is in a bubble of over-the-top spending that may not produce the profits and productivity that would make it all worth it. Elsewhere, Elon Musk’s blockbuster civil trial began in California. The drops came just a day before several of the biggest spenders on AI are scheduled to report their latest results for the start of 2026. They could offer more clues on whether all the investment in AI is producing the kind of returns that shareholders care about. Alphabet, Amazon, Meta Platforms and Microsoft are all reporting their latest quarterly results on Wednesday. Also weighing on the stock market was another rise for oil prices on continued uncertainty about what will happen with the Iran war.



The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil to be delivered in June climbed 2.8 per cent to settle at $US111.26. Brent to be delivered in July, which is where more of the trading is happening in the oil market, rose 2.7 per cent to $US104.40. After sitting around $US70 in late February, Brent prices are moving closer to their peak of $US119 reached when worries about the war have been at their heights. The focus is on the Strait of Hormuz, whose effective closure is keeping oil tankers stuck in the Persian Gulf instead of heading to customers worldwide. The Trump administration seemed unlikely Tuesday to accept Iran’s offer to reopen the Strait of Hormuz if the US lifts its blockade on the country. The proposal would postpone discussions on the Islamic Republic’s nuclear program, something that US Secretary of State Marco Rubio appeared to rule out in a Fox News interview on Monday. Meanwhile, the United Arab Emirates said it will leave OPEC effective May 1, stripping the oil cartel of its third-largest producer and further weakening its leverage over global oil supplies and prices.



The UAE’s decision had been rumoured as a possibility for some time, as it pushed back in recent years against OPEC production quotas it felt had been too low — meaning it wasn’t able to sell as much oil to the world as it had wanted. Meanwhile, the average price for a gallon of gasoline in the United States reached $US4.18 on Tuesday, the most since 2022, according to the auto club AAA. Expensive fuel was one of the reasons JetBlue Airways reported a worse loss for the start of 2026 than analysts expected. But its stock nevertheless rose 1.2 per cent after CEO Joanna Geraghty said the airline saw demand from customers strengthening through the quarter. JetBlue also announced moves to rein in fuel costs, such as cutting some flying. Another stock helping to limit Wall Street’s losses was Coca-Cola’s. It rallied 3.9 per cent after reporting stronger profit and revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected, thanks in part to strength from China, the United States and India.



All told, the S&P 500 fell 35.11 points to 7,138.80. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 25.86 to 49,141.93, and the Nasdaq composite sank 223.30 to 24,663.80. Related Article Opinion

Retail David Jones’ nail-biting escape from a near-death experience Elizabeth Knight Business columnist In the bond market, Treasury yields held relatively steady after a report showed US consumers are feeling slightly more confident in April, when economists expected to see a decline. The yield on the 10-year Treasury remained at 4.35 per cent, where it was late Monday. On Wednesday, the Federal Reserve is set to announce its latest decision on short-term interest rates. The widespread expectation is that it will hold the federal funds rate steady and hold off on resuming its cuts. Lower interest rates would help the economy, but they also risk worsening inflation when oil is expensive and tariffs are threatening to push prices higher. Also Wednesday, the Senate Banking Committee will vote on whether to confirm President Donald Trump’s nominee, Kevin Warsh, to succeed Fed Chair Jerome Powell. The committee is expected to approve Warsh and send his nomination to the full Senate.



In stock markets abroad, indexes fell across much of Europe and Asia. Japan’s Nikkei 225 sank 1 per cent for one of the world’s larger losses after the Bank of Japan opted in a split vote to keep its key interest rate unchanged. “There are various risks to the outlook,” it said in a statement. “For the time being it is necessary to pay particular attention to the impact of the future course of the situation in the Middle East.” AP The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. World.title: Ex-FBI chief charged with threatening the life of the president over Trump seashell post
World.content:
Breaking WorldNorth AmericaJames Comey Ex-FBI chief charged with threatening the life of the president over Trump seashell post Alanna Durkin Richer and Eric Tucker Updated April 29, 2026 — 6:16am ,first published 5:40am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Washington: Former FBI Director James Comey has been indicted again, this time in an investigation over a social media photo of seashells arranged on a beach that officials said constituted a threat against President Donald Trump. The two-count indictment charges Comey with “knowingly and wilfully” making a threat to “take the life of, and to inflict bodily harm upon” Trump and with transmitting a threat in interstate commerce. Former FBI director James Comey. AP It offers no evidence to support the claim that Comey knowingly made a threat against the president, especially since he has said the opposite, but suggested a “reasonable recipient who is familiar with the circumstances would interpret” the message as a threat to do harm. The criminal case is the second in a matter of months against Comey and is part of the Trump administration Justice Department’s relentless effort to prosecute political opponents of the Republican president.



The seashells photo was posted nearly a year ago, but the indictment was secured as acting Attorney General Todd Blanche – a Trump loyalist who previously served as his personal lawyer – aims to prove to the president that he’s the right person to hold the job permanently. The new case was filed in the Eastern District of North Carolina, the state where Comey found the seashells. The image from an Instagram post below which Comey wrote “cool shell formation on my beach walk”. nna\mikala.theocharous The fact that the Justice Department pursued a new case against the ex-FBI director months after a separate and unrelated indictment was dismissed could open the government to claims of a vindictive prosecution and to arguments that it is going out of its way to target Comey. Comey had overseen the early months of an investigation into whether the Republican president’s 2016 campaign had coordinated with Russia to sway the outcome of that year’s election. He was fired by Trump months into the president’s first term, and they have openly feuded ever since.



Comey’s lawyer did not immediately respond to a request seeking comment on Tuesday, and a Justice Department spokesperson did not immediately comment. Related Article Analysis

Trump's America It’s fine to call the US president a fascist or a despot – but this one line really rattled the White House The prosecution arises from a May post on Instagram in which Comey shared a photo of seashells he saw on a walk in the arrangement of “86 47”. He has said he assumed that the numbers reflected a political message, not a call to violence. Comey deleted the post shortly after it was made, writing: “I didn’t realize some folks associate those numbers with violence” and “I oppose violence of any kind so I took the post down.” Nonetheless, Comey was swiftly interviewed by the Secret Service after Trump administration officials asserted that he was advocating the assassination of Trump, the 47th president.



Merriam-Webster, the dictionary used by the AP, says 86 is slang meaning “to throw out”, “to get rid of” or “to refuse service to”. It notes: “Among the most recent senses adopted is a logical extension of the previous ones, with the meaning of ‘to kill.’ We do not enter this sense, due to its relative recency and sparseness of use.” Trump, in a Fox News Channel interview in May, accused Comey of knowing “exactly what that meant”. Acting Attorney-General Todd Blanche. AP “A child knows what that meant,” Trump said. “If you’re the FBI director and you don’t know what that meant, that meant assassination. And it says it loud and clear.” The former FBI director was indicted in September on charges that he lied to and obstructed Congress related to testimony he gave in 2020 about whether he had authorised inside information about an investigation to be provided to a journalist. He denied any wrongdoing, and the case was subsequently dismissed after a judge concluded that the prosecutor who brought the indictment was illegally appointed.



Comey was the FBI director when Trump took office in 2017, having been appointed by then-President Barack Obama, a Democrat, and serving before that as a senior Justice Department official in President George W. Bush’s Republican administration. Related Article Donald Trump Former FBI director Comey questioned over social media ‘threat’ to Trump But the relationship was strained from the start, including after Comey resisted a request by Trump at a private dinner to pledge his personal loyalty to the president – an overture that so unnerved the FBI director that he documented it in a contemporaneous memorandum. Trump fired Comey in May 2017 amid an FBI investigation into potential ties between Russia and Trump’s presidential campaign. That inquiry, later taken over by special counsel Robert Mueller, would ultimately find that while Russia interfered in the 2016 election and the Trump team welcomed the help, there was insufficient evidence to prove a criminal collaboration. Blanche was elevated earlier this month from deputy attorney general to acting attorney general, replacing Pam Bondi, who had frustrated Trump with the department’s struggles to build successful criminal cases against his adversaries.



Blanche since then has moved quickly to announce politically charged prosecutions, including a case last week against the nonprofit Southern Poverty Law Centre, which is accused by the Justice Department of defrauding donors by paying donors to infiltrate hate groups. The group has denied any wrongdoing. Related Article US politics ‘Not a call to assassination’: Kimmel defends Melania gag after Trumps demand his firing Comey is among many Trump foes to face scrutiny over the last year. The Justice Department, for instance, is also pursuing a criminal investigation into former CIA Director John Brennan, another key figure in the Russia investigation – one of Trump’s chief grievances and a saga that he and his supporters have long sought retaliation for. Brennan has denied doing anything wrong. Meanwhile, the Federal Communications Commission will start an early review of the TV station licenses owned by Walt Disney’s ABC network over potential “unlawful discrimination” the regulator said Tuesday.



In a two-page order from the FCC’s Media Bureau, the eight Disney-owned stations are directed to file license renewals by May 28 – at least two years earlier than otherwise required. The unusual move comes just a day after Trump told ABC to fire late-night host Jimmy Kimmel over a joke he made last week about the US first lady having the glow of an “expectant widow”, escalating pressure from the US government on the media. The review is tied to the commission’s inquiry last year into Disney’s diversity, equity and inclusion practices and whether they were discriminatory. FCC Chairman Brendan Carr has reviewed evidence leading him to believe that the company has given employees different opportunities based on their race and gender, according to a person familiar with the matter, who asked to not be identified because the discussions are private. In that context, Carr believes it’s appropriate to accelerate the license renewal process and evaluate whether ABC is operating the stations in the public interest, the person said. World.title: Are you ready for Australia’s $5 trillion wealth transfer?
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessBanking & financeSuperannuation Are you ready for Australia’s $5 trillion wealth transfer? Brought to you by Aware Super Cameron Bayley April 29, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Our team of financial experts help you navigate to and through retirement in this six-part series. See all stories .

With an estimated $5 trillion dollars set to be passed onto the next generation in coming decades, Australians are being urged to think seriously about estate planning. “We’re on the cusp of one of the largest wealth transfers we’ve ever seen,” explains Peter Hogg, general manager guidance and advice at Aware Super. “That’s driven by an ageing population, rising asset values, house prices and superannuation.” Keeping your will up-to-date is of crucial importance. iStock When to make a will It’s common to think you need a certain level of wealth before bothering to make a will, but that’s not the case, Hogg explains.





How to make a will Aware Super’s Peter Hogg There are several ways to make a legal will, but it’s important to be aware that different states can have slightly different regulations. “One of the biggest myths about estate planning is that it’s really expensive and complex,” says Hogg. “And, sure, there are areas where it can get a bit more complex, but for many Australians having a straightforward will can significantly reduce risk and make sure you’re in control.”



Options range from very basic DIY templates that can be downloaded for free, or kits available to purchase online, or engaging a solicitor, which can be especially important in more complex scenarios. Adam Lubofsky, the founder of online will company Safewill says even if your situation seems straightforward, you’re doing a huge favour for those you leave behind by fulfilling this responsibility. “It is going to be more expensive and more time-consuming if there is no will in place,” he says. If you die without a will, called ‘dying intestate’, the government dictates who receives your assets. And once you start the task, you may find there’s more you want to cover than you first imagine. “At Safewill we’ve seen a lot of personalised instructions,” Lubofsky adds. “Whether that’s funeral wishes, specifying exactly what you want your send-off to look like; or pet-care provision; or specific gifts and assets to your loved ones; or leaving part of your estate to charity.”



Adam Lubofsky. Keep it updated Writing a will is one thing, keeping it current across life events and stages is another. “A will is not a ‘set and forget’, ” Lubofsky cautions. In fact, several life circumstances impact the validity of a will, like marriage or divorce … so making sure that you keep it up-to-date is of utmost importance.” “Because if you write a will that isn’t valid at the time it’s surfaced, there isn’t that much point to it.”



Hogg agrees, saying ease of amending documents is crucial: “We would expect that over the course of someone’s life, they might update their estate planning a number of times.” Related Article Sponsored

Superannuation How to calculate your ‘magic retirement number’ Remember - super is different An often-overlooked aspect of estate planning is how super is treated. “Superannuation doesn’t automatically form part of your estate and that means it doesn’t automatically go to your dependents,” Hogg explains. “Your super is paid to the beneficiary nomination named in your super fund, so that makes that a really critical part of the process.”



There are rules around who you can nominate for this role, so check with your super fund – but the process is generally simple. “For our members, you can do it online,” Hogg explains. “It’s called a ‘binding non-lapsing nomination’ so it doesn’t expire, and it takes just five minutes.” Advice given in this article is general in nature and is not intended to influence readers’ decisions about investing or financial products. They should always seek their own professional advice that takes into account their own personal circumstances before making any financial decisions.
